section.title: One Sacrifice Once for All
section.sectionRationale: The writer brings the priestly argument to its climax. The law's endlessly repeated sacrifices could never take away sins or perfect the worshiper; they were only a shadow. Christ came to do God's will, offering His body once for all. By that single offering He has perfected forever those being sanctified, and where sins are forgiven, no further offering is needed.
section.thesis: The law's repeated sacrifices, being only a shadow, could never take away sins or perfect the worshiper; but Christ came to do God's will and by the single offering of His body has sanctified His people and perfected forever those being sanctified, so that, sins being forgiven, no further sacrifice for sin remains.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the law's shadow and its powerless, repeated sacrifices; Christ's coming to do God's will, offering His body once for all; and the finality of that one offering, which perfects forever and, with forgiveness secured, ends all sacrifice for sin.

verses.text: For the law is only a {{skia|shadow}} of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship.
If it could, would not the offerings have ceased? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt the guilt of their sins.
Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins,
because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

units.label: A body You prepared for Me
units.note: I have come to do Your will

verses.text: Therefore, when Christ came into the world, He said: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me.
In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight.
Then I said, ‘Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.’”
In the passage above He says, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not desire, nor did You delight in them” (although they are offered according to the law).
Then He adds, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” He takes away the first to establish the second.
And by that will, we have been {{hagiazo|sanctified}} through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ {{ephapax|once for all}}.
Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.
But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.
Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet,
because by a single offering He has made {{teleioo|perfect}} for all time those who are being sanctified.
The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First He says:
“This is the covenant I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.”
Then He adds: “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.”
And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.

skia.gloss: A shadow, the faint outline cast by a coming reality. The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, not the substance; its repeated sacrifices could sketch but never supply the true removal of sins.

hagiazo.gloss: To sanctify, to make holy, to set apart for God. By God's will, believers have been sanctified through the once-for-all offering of Christ's body, both decisively set apart and progressively made holy.

ephapax.gloss: Once for all, at a single decisive moment never to be repeated. Christ's body was offered once for all, in stark contrast to the daily and yearly sacrifices that had to be endlessly repeated.

teleioo.gloss: To make perfect, complete, fully fit to draw near to God. By a single offering Christ has perfected forever those being sanctified, giving them a completed standing before God that the law never could.

basic.context: This is the summit of the letter's argument about sacrifice. The law's sacrifices, offered year after year, could never actually take away sins; they only reminded people of them. They were a shadow of the real thing. Then Christ came, saying in the words of Psalm 40 that God desired not sacrifices but obedience, and He offered His own body once for all. By that single offering He has perfected His people forever, and where there is forgiveness, no more sacrifice is needed.
basic.hermeneutics: Watch the contrast between 'again and again' and 'once for all', and between the priests who stand and Christ who sat down. The quotation of Psalm 40 supplies the logic: God always wanted obedience, fulfilled in Christ's willing self-offering.
basic.originalLanguages: The law is a skia, shadow. By Christ's offering we are hagiazō, sanctified, ephapax, once for all. By a single offering He has teleioō, perfected, those being sanctified.
basic.typology: The whole sacrificial system, the daily offerings and the Day of Atonement, is the shadow whose substance is Christ's one offering. Psalm 40's obedient servant is fulfilled in the Son who comes to do God's will.
basic.christ: Christ is the one who came to do God's will and offered His body once for all. Unlike the priests who stand and repeat their work, He sat down, His sacrifice finished, and by one offering He perfects His people forever.
basic.god: God did not ultimately desire animal sacrifices but the obedience they pointed to, supplied by His Son. God's will is the ground of our sanctification, and God Himself declares that He will remember our sins no more.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 40 supplies the quotation. Psalm 110 gives the enthronement. Jeremiah 31 provides the forgiveness of the new covenant.
basic.oneStory: The endless sacrifices of the old covenant always testified that sin was not yet truly removed; the story reaches its goal in Christ's one offering, which takes sin away and perfects His people forever.

context.literary:
Hebrews 10:1-18 is the closing movement of a long argument that began at 8:1 and is built like a frame. Chapter 8 quoted the promise of a new covenant from Jeremiah 31 in full. Chapter 9 explained the old tent and the new. Here the writer returns to the same Jeremiah text, cites only its two crowning clauses, and draws the conclusion in verse 18. The block therefore begins and ends on the same theme, which is the removal of sin, and ties the whole central section of the letter into one package.

Inside the passage the writer works by pairs. Verses 1 to 4 describe the law and its sacrifices, and verses 5 to 10 give the speech of Christ. Verses 11 to 14 set the priest who stands against the priest who sits, and verses 15 to 18 add the testimony of the Holy Spirit. Verses 8 and 9 do something unusual: they read back a quotation just given, phrase by phrase, and explain which part is cancelled and which part is established. That is the technique of a preacher who expects his hearers to have the text in front of them.

There is also a deliberate play on repetition. 'Year after year,' 'day after day,' 'again and again' crowd verses 1 to 11, and then verse 12 answers with 'one sacrifice' and 'for all time.' The sentence structure changes with the theme. The old order is described in long, circling sentences; the new arrives in short ones, 'He sat down,' 'He waits,' 'no longer needed.'

Finally, verse 18 works as a hinge. It ends the doctrine, and the little word 'therefore' at 10:19 turns everything just taught into an appeal, so that the sacrifice described here becomes the ground of the invitation that follows.
context.historical:
The readers are most likely Jewish believers who lived near the pressure of a working sacrificial system. The letter speaks in the present tense of priests who 'stand' and 'offer,' and the writer never says the temple has fallen, which is one reason many place the letter before the year 70. Whatever the date, the daily rhythm in verse 11 is real life to these people: a morning and an evening offering each day, and the one day in the year when the high priest alone entered the inner sanctuary, as Leviticus 16 lays out.

That annual ritual explains verse 3. The Day of Atonement was set aside once a year, and Leviticus 16:34 says it was to be kept 'once a year' for all the sins of Israel. The writer reads the calendar itself as evidence. A sacrifice that must be scheduled again next year is a sacrifice that did not finish the matter, and the worshiper went home, as verse 2 says, still carrying a conscience that needed relief.

The repeated offerings also stood in a world where sacrifice was assumed almost everywhere. Pagan neighbours offered to many gods, and Jewish worship offered to one, but in both settings the idea that blood given in the right way could secure favour was familiar. The writer does not mock that world. He grants that the law's sacrifices were commanded, as he says in verse 8, and he builds on the point that they pointed beyond themselves.

The quotation from Psalm 40 would also have sounded like David's voice in the mouths of Greek speaking readers, since the writer uses the Septuagint form, which reads 'a body You prepared for Me.' The first hearers, who knew the psalms by singing them, would have recognised the song and been startled to hear it placed on the lips of Christ at His coming into the world.
context.canonical:
Three Old Testament passages carry the weight of this section, and the writer takes them in the order of Scripture's own history: law, psalm, prophet. The law supplies the pattern of repeated sacrifice, in Leviticus 1 to 7 and above all in Leviticus 16. The psalm supplies the voice of the one who says, 'I have come,' Psalm 40:7. The prophet supplies the promise of a covenant written on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33-34.

The prophets and psalms had long hinted that sacrifice was never the whole point. Samuel told Saul that 'obedience is better than sacrifice,' 1 Samuel 15:22. Psalm 51 says God takes no delight in sacrifice and then asks for a broken spirit, Psalm 51:16-17, and Micah 6:6-8 asks whether the Lord is pleased with thousands of rams and answers by naming justice, mercy and humble walking. Hebrews gathers these scattered signals into one sharp claim: the law's sacrifices were never designed to be the final answer.

The verse that crowns the section, 'He sat down at the right hand of God,' turns to Psalm 110:1, a text the writer has used since 1:13. The writer reads it as the end of the priestly work: the sitting of verse 12 and the waiting of verse 13 are lifted from it.

Later in the New Testament, the same finality is announced in other voices. John records Jesus saying 'It is finished,' John 19:30. Paul writes that Christ died to sin 'once for all,' Romans 6:10, and Peter that Christ 'suffered once for sins,' 1 Peter 3:18. Hebrews supplies the argument that explains why those short confessions are true.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his wavering readers to see that going back to the old sacrificial order is not a safe retreat but a step down from the real thing to its shadow. He is not criticising the law, which he grants was given by God, verse 8. His point is that a system built on repetition was honestly designed to point forward, and that the thing it pointed to has now arrived.

He also wants them to see the sacrifice of Christ as an act of obedience and not merely an act of suffering. By placing Psalm 40 in Christ's mouth, he shows a Son who speaks to the Father before He acts, 'I have come to do Your will,' and who offers His body because He was willing, not because He was dragged. That makes the cross a conversation inside God before it is a wound on a man.

Third, he wants them to feel what finality means for the conscience. Verse 2 names the real aim, which is that worshipers should 'no longer have felt the guilt of their sins.' The goal is a cleansed inner life, not a cleaner calendar. The readers who are tempted to drift are meant to hear that nothing more needs to be added, and that the one thing left is to draw near, which is exactly where chapter 10 goes next.

Last, he wants the covenant promise of Jeremiah to be received as a present reality: laws written inwardly, sins forgotten. The Holy Spirit is brought in as a witness, verse 15, so that the readers know this is not the writer's private opinion but the testimony of Scripture as the Spirit speaks it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what the law's sacrifices did and what Christ's sacrifice did; it commands very little. It does not instruct anyone to stop reading Leviticus, and it does not say the old sacrifices were evil. It says they were commanded and that they pointed beyond themselves.

The practical consequence is carefully drawn. Since the one offering is complete, believers are not to try to add to it, whether by rituals, by penance, or by a private sense that they must make up what is lacking. To do so quietly denies verse 14. At the same time, the passage never teaches that the forgiven may sin lightly. The same writer warns in 10:26 that deliberate rejection of the only sacrifice leaves nothing else. The sacrifice finishes sin's penalty, and it is also the means by which God's laws get written on hearts, verse 16, which means holy living follows from it and does not compete with it.

Care is needed with the language of 'a body You prepared.' It describes what the Son did at His coming; it is not a pattern for the believer to repeat in the same way. What believers are invited to imitate is the posture, 'I have come to do Your will,' not the atoning work itself, which is done and cannot be repeated.

debates.question: How can believers be 'perfected forever' and yet 'being sanctified' at the same time?

views.label: A completed standing with an ongoing process
views.case: Verse 14 holds together a perfect, finished standing before God given once by Christ's offering, and an ongoing work of being made holy in daily life; the one secures the other. The verb for perfected is in the perfect tense and the participle for being sanctified is in the present, which fits a settled result alongside a continuing work.

views.label: Perfected in conscience and access, growing in holiness
views.case: The perfecting refers chiefly to the cleansed conscience and settled access to God, while sanctification is the continuing transformation into holiness, both flowing from the single offering. Verse 10 speaks of having been sanctified once for all, so 'sanctified' itself can describe a past act as well as a process.

debates.bearing: Both affirm that our acceptance before God rests wholly on Christ's finished work, even as His Spirit continues to make us holy; assurance and growth are not rivals.

debates.question: Why does the writer quote 'a body You prepared for Me' when the Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 speaks of ears?

views.label: The Septuagint wording, used faithfully
views.case: The writer quotes the Greek translation his readers knew. The Hebrew text speaks of ears being opened or dug for the speaker, a picture of the obedient listening servant; the Greek translators rendered it 'a body,' perhaps spreading the picture of a listening ear to the whole person. The writer takes the form he has and builds on it, since the point, an obedient servant who has a body to give, stands in either reading.

views.label: An inspired reading that draws out the meaning
views.case: Others hold that the Holy Spirit, who speaks through the text as verse 15 says, guided the writer to a wording that makes the fulfilment explicit. The ear that hears God's will is the very body offered at the cross, and the writer's point is not a textual argument but a theological one, that obedience and offering are the same act in Christ.

views.label: A deliberate emphasis on the incarnation
views.case: A third view stresses that the verse chiefly serves the writer's wider theme that the Son took flesh and blood, as in 2:14. The body of verse 5 and the body of verse 10 hold the passage together, and the writer would have wanted the word on the page whichever form of the psalm he found.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the writer's argument does not depend on a small difference in wording: the psalm says that God's real desire is obedience, and Hebrews says that obedience has a body and has been offered.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 calls the law a shadow, skia, and then says it is 'not the realities themselves.' The Greek is sharper than the English. The writer says the law has a shadow of good things to come and not 'the very image' of the realities, using eikon. A shadow is a dark outline cast by a solid object; an image is the full likeness. The law, then, is less than even a portrait. It is the outline cast by something not yet in the room. The same word skia appears at 8:5, where the tabernacle is a copy and shadow of heavenly things, and Colossians 2:17 uses it of festivals and sabbaths, a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ.

Verse 3 calls the sacrifices an 'annual reminder of sins,' where 'reminder' is anamnesis. This is the same noun Jesus used at the supper, 'in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19. The contrast is pointed. The old sacrifices recalled sins every year; the new covenant meal recalls a Saviour, and Jeremiah's promise in verse 17 says God will 'remember no more.' Verse 2 adds that worshipers would have 'no longer have felt the guilt of their sins,' using suneidesis, conscience, the inner witness that testifies to what a person has done. The writer's concern throughout this part of the letter is the conscience, which he says the blood of Christ cleanses at 9:14.

Verse 5 reads 'a body You prepared for Me.' The verb is katartizo, which means to fit, mend or put in order, the word used of mending nets, Matthew 4:21. A body was fitted for the Son. That sets the incarnation inside the psalm: the body is not an accident but a preparation.

Verse 10 has 'we have been sanctified,' a periphrastic perfect, with ephapax, 'once for all,' at the end. Ephapax is the writer's favourite word for finality, found at 7:27 and 9:12 and in Paul at Romans 6:10. Verse 14 balances this with two tenses: the perfect tense for 'has made perfect,' teteleiōken, and the present participle for 'those who are being sanctified.' The first is a completed act with lasting result; the second describes people still on the way. The verb teleioo, 'to make perfect,' carries the sense of bringing to its goal or fitting for access, and in this letter it is chiefly about being brought into God's presence with a clean conscience.

Verse 11 says the priest 'stands,' and the perfect tense hestēken describes a standing posture that has never changed, because there is no seat in the tabernacle. Verse 12 answers with the aorist 'sat down,' ekathisen. One tense speaks of habitual standing; the other of a single completed act that ends in rest. The verb leitourgeo, 'to minister,' in verse 11 is the root of our word liturgy.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement and its annual repetition, Leviticus 16
typology.fulfillment: Once a year the high priest entered the inner sanctuary with the blood of a bull and a goat, Leviticus 16:14-15, and the people waited outside. Hebrews reads the yearly return as the very mark of incompleteness, verse 3. In Christ the pattern is brought to its goal: He enters not an earthly tent but the presence of God, and does so once, Hebrews 9:24-26. The escalation is from animal to person, from yearly to once for all, from a veil that kept people out to a way opened through it. The type falls short in that it could only remind; it could not remove, verse 4.

typology.type: The standing priest and the seated Christ, verses 11 and 12
typology.fulfillment: Nothing in the tabernacle furniture provided a seat, because the priest's work was never done. The Christ of this passage does what no priest could do and sits down. His seat is not idleness but completion, and it is the same seat promised to David's Lord in Psalm 110:1. The New Testament extends the picture: the Son sits and waits for His enemies to be made a footstool, verse 13, and believers are raised with Him and seated with Him, Ephesians 2:6. The type falls short because the priests were themselves sinners who offered first for their own sins, Hebrews 7:27, while this Priest has no sin of His own to atone for.

typology.type: The obedient servant of Psalm 40, verses 5 to 9
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist speaks as one who delights to do God's will and carries the scroll of it within, Psalm 40:8. The writer hears that voice as the Son's, and the pattern of faithful obedience in the psalm is brought to its full form in Jesus, who came 'not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me,' John 6:38. In Gethsemane He prays 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The correspondence is real, but the psalm's singer could only offer thanks and praise; the Son offers a body and takes sin away. Paul says that Christ 'became obedient to death,' Philippians 2:8, and that through one man's obedience the many will be made righteous, Romans 5:19.

typology.type: The covenant written on hearts, verses 16 and 17
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai the law was cut into stone tablets, Exodus 31:18, and was external to the people who had to keep it. Jeremiah promised a day when God would put His law in minds and hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, and Ezekiel pictured a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. Hebrews says that day has come with the Holy Spirit's witness to Christ's offering. Paul describes the church as 'a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3. The type still points forward in one respect: the work of inscribing continues until believers are fully conformed to the Son, 1 John 3:2.

study.christ:
The passage brings us to Christ chiefly by presenting Him as the speaker of Scripture. Verses 5 to 7 introduce the quotation with 'when Christ came into the world, He said,' and the Greek verb is in the present tense, as though the psalm is the Son's own word to the Father at the threshold of the incarnation. The writer is claiming that before Bethlehem, in some sense, the Son already spoke the words 'I have come,' and that David was given them in advance. This is a high Christology in short compass: the Son who comes is the same Son who speaks, who has a will that agrees with the Father's, and who takes a body prepared for Him.

The passage presents the work of Christ as both priestly and obedient. The priestly side is the offering of 'the body of Jesus Christ once for all,' verse 10. The obedient side is the repeated 'I have come to do Your will,' verses 7 and 9. These are not two stories but one. The sacrifice has value because it is the obedience of a willing Son, as Paul puts it, 'He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8. Where the old sacrifices were substituted by animals who knew nothing of the exchange, here the one who is offered is the one who offers and the one who chooses.

The sitting of verse 12 points to His present reign and His finished work together. He sat down at the right hand of God, and He waits, verse 13, for the last enemies to become a footstool, which links the work on the cross to the final victory described in 1 Corinthians 15:25-26. The One who sits is not passive. He intercedes, Hebrews 7:25, and He rules.

The effects of His offering are named in the three verbs 'sanctified,' 'made perfect,' and 'forgiven.' The first speaks of being set apart for God, the second of being fitted for His presence, and the third of the debt being cancelled. John's first letter says that 'the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin,' 1 John 1:7, and Hebrews shows why that is true and not merely hoped.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage does not say that every sacrifice in Leviticus is a coded picture of one detail of the crucifixion. It says that, taken together, the repeated sacrifices could not do what they appeared to promise, and that Christ did it. The link is from inadequacy to fulfilment, not from detail to detail. What is certain is the meeting point: His body, offered once, in obedience, with the Holy Spirit's testimony, ends the need for any further offering for sin.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who does not want what He is commonly thought to want. People in every age assume that the divine can be bought off, and the old sacrificial law looked, to a careless eye, like a system for doing exactly that. Verses 5 and 6 say plainly that God did not desire sacrifice and offering, and took no delight in burnt offerings and sin offerings. The God of this chapter wants a people who do His will from the heart, and He has moved heaven and earth to supply what He asked for.

He is a God with a plan, not an emergency measure. The psalm is quoted as having been written beforehand, and the phrase 'it is written about Me in the scroll' places the incarnation inside a design carried through Scripture. Hebrews 2:10 says it was fitting for the God for whom and through whom all things exist to bring many sons to glory through suffering. The cross is not the failure of an earlier arrangement but the fulfilment of a long intention.

He is a God who speaks in three voices that agree. The Son speaks in verses 5 to 9, the Holy Spirit testifies in verse 15, and the Father is the one to whom the Son speaks and who says 'I will remember no more.' The doctrine of the Trinity is not argued here, but the passage assumes it. The Father prepares the body, the Son comes to do His will, and the Spirit bears witness, and the three are one in giving salvation.

He is just, and He is merciful, and the passage holds both. Verse 4 says it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins, which means sin is real, not a ritual oversight that can be waved away. Verse 17 says He will remember sins no more, which means mercy is real too. The two meet at the single offering, where the penalty is paid and the record cleared. As Romans 3:26 says, God is both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus.

He is a God who writes. Verse 16 says He puts His laws on hearts and inscribes them on minds. The verbs are the verbs of a craftsman, not of a distant lawgiver. He works inwardly on those He forgives.

For worship, this means we can come with confidence, not with a nervous eye on a calendar. The God who forgets our sins in the sense of no longer holding them against us is the God before whom we may sit, as His Son has sat, and rest. It also means gratitude: the forgiveness we enjoy was not cheap, and it was God's own provision, not our bargaining.

crossReferences.note: The source of the quotation in verses 5 to 7. In Hebrew the singer says that ears were opened for him; Hebrews follows the Greek 'a body.' Either way the psalm sets obedience above sacrifice and puts the will of God written on the heart of the speaker. Hebrews hears the voice of the Son.

The law of the Day of Atonement says it is to be kept once a year to make atonement for the Israelites for all their sins. Hebrews takes the yearly return as proof of the system's limit, in verse 3, and sets against it a single offering for all time.
Samuel tells Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice. Hebrews 10 gathers this prophetic strand and shows its end: what God sought in sacrifice was obedience, and Christ supplies it in full.

The enthronement verse behind verses 12 and 13. The Lord says to David's Lord, 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' Hebrews reads the sitting as the end of priestly labour and the waiting as the interval before final victory.

The new covenant promise cited in verses 16 and 17: laws on hearts, and sins remembered no more. Hebrews takes the second clause as the basis of verse 18, that where sins are forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.

The sister passage in the previous chapter. Christ does not offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters year by year with blood not his own, but appears once at the end of the ages to put away sin by His sacrifice. The two chapters interlock.

Paul's short statement that the death Christ died, He died to sin once for all. It uses the same word, ephapax, that Hebrews relies on. Paul draws a lesson for the believer's life, and Hebrews draws one for the believer's conscience.

Jesus' cry, 'It is finished.' The Gospel uses a verb of completion and Hebrews supplies the argument for why completion is the right word. Everything the Levitical priests could not finish, the cross finished.

A parallel promise to Jeremiah's: a new heart, a new spirit, and God's own Spirit within. It shows that the inscribing of verse 16 is not an extra to forgiveness but the same covenant gift applied inwardly.

Paul calls festivals, new moons and sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ. It is the same shadow and substance logic as Hebrews 10:1, applied to the whole calendar of the old law.

study.oneStory:
From the first chapters of Genesis, the story of Scripture has asked how a holy God can live among a sinful people. After the fall, God clothed the pair from the skin of an animal, Genesis 3:21, and Abel's offering from the flock was accepted, Genesis 4:4. Noah offered burnt offerings after the flood, Genesis 8:20, and Abraham raised an altar at each stage of his journey. By Sinai the pattern had grown into a detailed system, with a tent, a priesthood, daily offerings and one great day each year. All of it said the same thing: sin is serious, life must be given, and the way back to God is guarded.

Yet the system itself kept pointing past its own limits. A sacrifice was repeated because it did not finish, the priest stood because the work was never done, and the veil hung because the way was not yet open. The prophets sharpened the point, saying that God wanted mercy and not sacrifice, Hosea 6:6, and that a day was coming when a new covenant would be made, with sins forgotten, Jeremiah 31:34. The story was being tightened toward a person.

Hebrews 10 is the place where Scripture itself says the knot is untied. The Son, who speaks in the psalm, comes into the world, takes the body prepared for Him, does the Father's will and offers that body once. The long line of altars ends in one. The line of priests ends in one who sits. The promise of Jeremiah moves from forecast to fact.

What the passage sets up is the life of the people of the new covenant. Because the offering is done, the readers can draw near, hold fast, and spur one another on, as the next section urges. The same truth underlies the church's meal, in which Christ's body and blood are remembered rather than repeated, and the church's mission, in which the news that sins are forgiven is carried to all nations, Luke 24:47.

The story closes in the new creation, where there is no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The work of sacrifice is finished, the enemies have become a footstool, and the people whose hearts were written on by God dwell with Him. The shadow has lifted because the substance is here, and the sun does not set, Revelation 21:23.

quiz.q: Why could the law's sacrifices never truly deal with sin?

options.text: They were only a shadow, and it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
They were offered by the wrong people.
options.note: The problem was not the personnel but the inability of animal blood to remove sins.

options.text: They had to be repeated endlessly, year after year.
options.note: Their constant repetition did expose their weakness, but the root reason is that animal blood simply cannot take away sins.

options.text: They actually did take away sins fully.
options.note: The passage says they could not take away sins.

quiz.q: What did Christ say, in the words of Psalm 40, when He came into the world?

options.text: Sacrifice You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me; I have come to do Your will.
That He came to do God's will, fulfilling what was written of Him.
options.note: This is true and part of the quotation, whose fuller point is that God desired obedience, not sacrifice, and a body was prepared for Christ.

options.text: That God delights in burnt offerings above all.
options.note: The quotation says God took no delight in them.

options.text: That He came only to teach.
options.note: He came to do God's will by offering His body, not merely to teach.

quiz.q: What has Christ accomplished by His single offering?

options.text: He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.
He has sanctified His people through the offering of His body.
options.note: True, from verse 10, and verse 14 adds that by that single offering He has perfected them forever.

options.text: He has left the work unfinished.
options.note: He sat down, His sacrifice complete.

options.text: He has perfected only those who never sin again.
options.note: He perfects those being sanctified, who are still growing in holiness.

quiz.q: What follows from God's promise to remember our sins no more?

options.text: Where there is forgiveness, an offering for sin is no longer needed.
We must keep offering sacrifices to be safe.
options.note: No further offering is needed once sins are forgiven.
The forgiveness is settled; God remembers our sins no more.

options.text: Our sins are fully forgiven, though we still confess them.
options.note: Forgiveness is complete, which is the point; the verse draws the further conclusion that no offering for sin is any longer needed.

questions: Christ has perfected forever those being sanctified. How does holding a finished standing before God together with ongoing growth free you from both pride and despair?
The priests stood and repeated their work; Christ sat down. What does His sitting down tell you about the completeness of His work for you?
God says He will remember your sins no more. Do you live as one truly forgiven, or do you keep re-offering for sins God has already forgotten?
Christ came to do God's will. How does His willing obedience shape your own obedience to the Father?
No further offering for sin is needed. What self-made sacrifices or penances might you be adding to Christ's finished work?

translationNotes.note: The quotation of Psalm 40 reads 'a body You prepared for Me', following the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads 'ears You have opened for Me', both pointing to wholehearted obedience.
'Made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified' holds a completed perfect tense and an ongoing present participle together, uniting a finished standing with a continuing work.
'Shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves' contrasts skia, shadow, with the true form; the law sketches what only Christ supplies.
